34a9b8a33d25d635.paragraph: When an RL researcher and an LLM-agent builder say *agent*, they name different objects, and claims that cross between them arrive with the words but not the objects: a deployed LLM agent is said to hack a reward it does not have. This paper lays the two meanings side by side, one primitive at a time, in training and in deployment, and says where each word keeps its meaning and where it loses it. It describes the gap and proposes no bridge. One culture writes down the decision process and the reward and learns a policy; the other prompts a pretrained model inside a scaffold with tools and judges it by what it does. We take the eight primitives that @sutton2018 define, reward, policy, action, observation, state, transition, episode and value, and read each one in nine settings: an RL agent in training and in deployment, chat training with an outcome reward model, with a verifier and with a process reward model, agent training with trajectory reward, and deployment of a chatbot, of a tool agent with a human between steps and of an autonomous tool agent. The reading is a table of 72 cells, each with its reason and sources. We also code 23 properties in every setting and compare settings only within a phase. In training and in deployment alike, LLM agents differ from RL agents on four properties, among them that an LLM agent's observations can carry instructions and its behaviour can be steered through its input. In deployment the RL agent's task still has a reward function and the LLM's has none. Some differences that look cultural are differences of phase: neither a deployed RL policy nor a deployed LLM uses reward to change its parameters. Chat training with a learned or programmatic outcome reward is a contextual bandit with no subsequent decision and a degenerate value; process supervision is the LLM training setting closest to RL training on four properties, though its dense reward is a learned score. @breiman2001 described the same split in statistics, between a culture that assumes a stochastic model of the inside of the box and one that treats the inside as unknown and judges by prediction. We set the two cultures of agents in his lines, measure how little the two literatures cite each other, and say which of his discussants' objections transfer: Cox's on prediction under changed conditions, Efron's on prediction being only occasionally sufficient, and Hoadley's on constraints engineered around a model that is not read from the inside.

e3dfff4ecace5f00.paragraph: No prior paper reads the RL primitives setting by setting for LLM systems, or sets the RL-agent culture against the LLM-agent culture. The nearest work comes in four strands. First, the formal reading of RLHF as a bandit: @ahmadian2024 argue that the whole generation should be modelled as a single action and the problem reduces to a bandit; @li2024 drop the value model for the same reason; @xiong2024 formalise RLHF as a KL-regularised contextual bandit; @lambert2025 contrasts the bandit and token-level MDP framings in a textbook. @rafailov2024 show that DPO nonetheless learns an implicit token-level Q-function. Second, the constrained reading of the KL penalty: @moskovitz2024 cast RLHF with several reward models as a constrained MDP with one constraint per reward model, and note that the KL coefficient already acts as a Lagrange multiplier, @gao2023 treat KL as a budget, and @korbak2022 give the competing Bayesian reading. Third, the papers that assert or test the identity between LLM agents and RL agents: @mclean2026 write the agent as a POMDP and offer RL safety tools; our companion paper examines the conditions those tools need [@debunking2026]; @cagatan2026 port the AI safety gridworlds to LLM agents and find specification gaming; @turner2022b argues that a trained policy need not be a reward optimiser. Fourth, Breiman's frame and its sequels: @breiman2001, @shmueli2010 on explaining versus predicting, @donoho2017 on the common task framework, @efron2020 on prediction against attribution, and @damour2021 on the Rashomon set. @bristow2023 call the ethics-versus-alignment split a caricature of binary camps and argue that there are more than two camps, while noting that the communities have distinct cultures and norms; our split is orthogonal to it.

9d9ebeb74616abf4.paragraph: Neither "RL" nor "LLM" is one setting. We split by phase, training or deployment, and then by how the decision problem is posed: what one action is, and where the reward, if any, comes from (Table \ref{tab:settings}). The RL agent appears twice, in training and as a deployed fixed policy. The training settings for chat differ by reward source: a learned reward model fit to human preferences [@christiano2017; @ouyang2022], a programmatic verifier of the final answer [@lambert2024; @deepseekai2025], or a process reward model that scores each reasoning step [@uesato2022; @lightman2024]. Agent training rewards a whole multi-turn trajectory of tool calls [@zhou2024b]. Deployment has no reward source; its LLM settings differ by whether a human sees each step. The companion paper uses the same phase split and a coarser posing [@debunking2026]; our D-AGENT-A and D-AGENT-X refine its D-AGENT, and our T-CHAT and T-RLVR refine its T-CHAT.

53916be8abb61d21.paragraph:
- **Reward.** In deployment, the RL agent's task still has a reward function, written by its designer, whether or not the frozen policy uses it; the deployed LLM's task has none, and its objective is the instruction in the context. Neither a deployed RL policy nor a deployed LLM uses reward to change its parameters; that difference is between training and deployment, not between the cultures. The reward model, verifier or process reward model is a training artefact: @mclean2026 say of the process reward model that once training is complete it "is no longer used" [@mclean2026], and note that the reward function "is somewhat different from training (updating the policy) to deployment (freezing the policy)" [@mclean2026]. What stands in its place is the instruction in the context, which any later text in the context can revise, and the user's acceptance after the fact.
- **Action and transition.** In T-CHAT and T-RLVR the whole reply is one action and generation leads directly to a terminal state with no subsequent decision: the problem is a contextual bandit [@ahmadian2024; @xiong2024]; the cited work treats RLHF, and we extend the reading to verifier rewards. PPO treats tokens as actions, but the reward is terminal. RLOO and ReMax show that the bandit view suffices and drop the critic [@ahmadian2024; @li2024]; GRPO also drops the critic [@shao2024]. Under process supervision an action is one reasoning step and the transition is deterministic: the agent is the dynamics. In the agent settings an action is a tool call and the transition is what the tool and the world do, which no party fully controls.
- **Observation and state.** In RL the observation is data from a sensor. In the LLM settings the observation is mostly text, and text carries instructions; agents may also receive images and other modalities. In the agent settings tool outputs arrive in the same stream as the user's instructions, and models do not reliably separate the two [@zverev2025; @greshake2023]. The state of a deployed agent includes world state it cannot see and the user's intent; @mclean2026 concede that the agent's inputs "cannot fully capture the true state of the world and the user's intents" [@mclean2026]. In deployment the context window is a bounded, lossy belief.
- **Episode and value.** Resets exist in training. Under process supervision any prefix can be resampled; in agent training the environment resets between tasks. A deployed RL environment may be designed to reset; no LLM deployment setting is. A chatbot's conversation ends, and a tool agent's side effects persist. In deployment neither culture uses a learned value function; in the LLM deployment settings verbal self-checks and retries stand in for it (search-augmented agents score continuations by reverting to earlier states, which a live deployment does not allow), and each probe is a real action with persistent effects.
- **Which settings differ.** Table \ref{tab:gap} codes 23 properties in every setting; two independent raters agreed on 197/207 codes (kappa 0.92), and an adjudicator settled the rest. Settings are compared only within a phase, so that a difference between training and deployment is never read as a difference between the cultures. In training and in deployment alike, every LLM setting differs from the RL setting on four properties: whether behaviour can be steered through the input, the action set is fixed and known, observations can carry instructions and third parties can author observations. In deployment, every LLM setting also differs from the RL setting on seven more: whether a reward function is defined for the task, reward arrives at every step, the environment computes the reward, observations include the agent's own outputs, the state includes a principal's intent, the environment resets by design and a value estimate selects actions. Whether reward changes the parameters and the parameters change differs between training and deployment in both cultures and not between them. Under process supervision dense reward, Markov prefix, known dynamics and free resets all hold, which is why process supervision is the LLM training setting closest to RL training on those four properties, although its dense reward is a learned process-reward-model score, not an environment signal, and it has no side effects. DeepSeek-R1 reports that it dropped a process reward model after unsuccessful attempts, citing reward hacking, costly step annotation and a more complex pipeline [@deepseekai2025]; @zhang2025 find annotation bias and inflated best-of-N scores in existing process reward models and release an improved one.

2b2023d23e3ee762.paragraph: Two research cultures have grown around the two ends of the table. One begins by positing what is inside the box: an optimiser of a reward R in a decision process the designer wrote down, from which value functions, policy gradients and designed exploration follow [@sutton2018; @schulman2017]. The other treats the inside as unknown: a pretrained model steered by a prompt and a scaffold, judged by what it does on tasks [@yao2023b; @schick2023; @kapoor2024]. @breiman2001 described the same split in statistics. His data-modeling culture begins "Assume that the data are generated by the following model" [@breiman2001]; he put "98% of all statisticians" [@breiman2001] in it; and his objection was that "The conclusions are about the model's mechanism, and not about nature's mechanism." [@breiman2001] His algorithmic culture "considers the inside of the box complex and unknown" [@breiman2001] and validates by predictive accuracy. Table \ref{tab:cultures} sets the four cultures in his lines. We call ours *objective-modeling* and *behavior-modeling*, by their move, not their tribe. The mapping runs the RL-agent culture to Breiman's statistics, not to his machine learning: the move that matters is positing a parametric model of the inside of the box, and an MDP with a reward is such a model. The mapping is of moves, not of people: the same researcher trains a chatbot with PPO in the morning and prompts a tool agent in the afternoon, and the settings table says which culture each act belongs to.

4077e3f4038c96fb.paragraph: Breiman guessed the sizes of his cultures. We measured contact between ours. From OpenAlex [@openalex2026] we built an RL-agent corpus and an LLM-agent corpus for 2012–2026 with general queries (Table \ref{tab:census_general}). Louvain communities on the union graph recover our labels with purity 0.98 on the 1250 works that have at least one citation link (570 isolated works are excluded); the corpora share zero works. A second census restricted to the safety sub-literatures of each culture, where contact should be highest, gives 0.13% and 0.23% of references crossing (snapshot in `080\_census`).

4f5ddf20bfd0356e.paragraph: Breiman had a shared scoreboard, test-set accuracy. Agents have task success on benchmarks, and the scoreboard is shared only inside the behavior-modeling culture. Cox's objection transfers directly: "Often the prediction is under quite different conditions from the data" [@breiman2001]. An agent trained in a sandbox with resets and benign tool outputs is deployed without them; the gap between T-AGENT and D-AGENT-X in Table \ref{tab:primitive_cells_deployment} is the gap Cox names. Efron's transfers: "Prediction by itself is only occasionally sufficient." [@breiman2001] A task-success rate says what the agent did on those tasks and nothing about the mechanism, which is what the objective-modeling culture wants to know. Breiman's own Rashomon Effect transfers too: many functions give about the same error rate, so a benchmark score does not identify the agent behind it [@breiman2001; @damour2021]. The analogue we take is Hoadley's. Fair, Isaac ran algorithmic-culture scorecards in production from the 1960s, built from interpretable variables, with constraints on the model's form (monotone scores, shrunken weights) that client demand, law and robustness "led to the concept of score engineering" [@breiman2001]. For agents the constraints sit in the scaffold rather than in the model: the tool set, the permissions and the prompt are what a deployer can write, and the model inside is not read. That placement is our analogy, not Hoadley's. The objective-modeling culture is right that a written constraint is what makes a box usable and wrong about where it must live; the behavior-modeling culture is right that the inside cannot be specified and wrong if it concludes that nothing can be written.

15052b2648af92d9.paragraph: No prior paper reads the RL primitives setting by setting for LLM systems, or sets the RL-agent culture against the LLM-agent culture. The nearest work comes in four strands. First, the formal reading of RLHF as a bandit: @ahmadian2024 argue that the whole generation should be modelled as a single action and the problem reduces to a bandit; @li2024 drop the value model for the same reason; @xiong2024 formalise RLHF as a KL-regularised contextual bandit; @lambert2025 contrasts the bandit and token-level MDP framings in a textbook. @rafailov2024 show that DPO nonetheless learns an implicit token-level Q-function. Second, the constrained reading of the KL penalty: @moskovitz2024 cast RLHF with several reward models as a constrained MDP with one constraint per reward model, and note that the KL coefficient already acts as a Lagrange multiplier, @gao2023 treat KL as a budget, and @korbak2022 give the competing Bayesian reading. Third, the papers that assert or test the identity between LLM agents and RL agents: @mclean2026 write the agent as a POMDP and offer RL safety tools; our companion paper examines the conditions those tools need [@debunking2026]; @cagatan2026 port the AI safety gridworlds to LLM agents and find specification gaming; @turner2022b argues that a trained policy need not be a reward optimiser. Fourth, Breiman's frame and its sequels: @breiman2001, @shmueli2010 on explaining versus predicting, @donoho2017 on the common task framework, @efron2020 on prediction against attribution, and @damour2021 on the Rashomon set. @bristow2023 call the ethics-versus-alignment split a caricature of binary camps and argue that there are more than two camps, while noting that the communities have distinct cultures and norms; our split is orthogonal to it.

64e0dd0ab38ef742.paragraph: We take the definitions from the textbook, so that an RL reader can check the starting point (Table \ref{tab:primitives}). The reward is "a received scalar signal (called reward)" [@sutton2018], "passing from the environment to the agent" [@sutton2018]; it is the designer's channel for "what you want achieved, not how you want it achieved" [@sutton2018]. "Formally, a policy is a mapping from states to probabilities of selecting each possible action." [@sutton2018] An episode ends in a terminal state "followed by a reset to a standard starting state" [@sutton2018], and the next one begins independently. The dynamics are a function p of the state and action. These are the objects we track.

- **Reward.** In deployment, the RL agent's task still has a reward function, written by its designer, whether or not the frozen policy uses it; the deployed LLM's task has none, and its objective is the instruction in the context. Neither a deployed RL policy nor a deployed LLM uses reward to change its parameters; that difference is between training and deployment, not between the cultures. The reward model, verifier or process reward model is a training artefact: @mclean2026 say of the process reward model that once training is complete it "is no longer used" [@mclean2026], and note that the reward function "is somewhat different from training (updating the policy) to deployment (freezing the policy)" [@mclean2026]. What stands in its place is the instruction in the context, which any later text in the context can revise, and the user's acceptance after the fact.
- **Action and transition.** In T-CHAT and T-RLVR the whole reply is one action and generation leads directly to a terminal state with no subsequent decision: the problem is a contextual bandit [@ahmadian2024; @xiong2024]; the cited work treats RLHF, and we extend the reading to verifier rewards. PPO treats tokens as actions, but the reward is terminal. RLOO and ReMax show that the bandit view suffices and drop the critic [@ahmadian2024; @li2024]; GRPO also drops the critic [@shao2024]. Under process supervision an action is one reasoning step and the transition is deterministic: the agent is the dynamics. In the agent settings an action is a tool call and the transition is what the tool and the world do, which no party fully controls.
- **Observation and state.** In RL the observation is data from a sensor. In the LLM settings the observation is mostly text, and text carries instructions; agents may also receive images and other modalities. In the agent settings tool outputs arrive in the same stream as the user's instructions, and models do not reliably separate the two [@zverev2025; @greshake2023]. The state of a deployed agent includes world state it cannot see and the user's intent; @mclean2026 concede that the agent's inputs "cannot fully capture the true state of the world and the user's intents" [@mclean2026]. In deployment the context window is a bounded, lossy belief.
- **Episode and value.** Resets exist in training. Under process supervision any prefix can be resampled; in agent training the environment resets between tasks. A deployed RL environment may be designed to reset; no LLM deployment setting is. A chatbot's conversation ends, and a tool agent's side effects persist. In deployment neither culture uses a learned value function; in the LLM deployment settings verbal self-checks and retries stand in for it (search-augmented agents score continuations by reverting to earlier states, which a live deployment does not allow), and each probe is a real action with persistent effects.
- **Which settings differ.** Table \ref{tab:gap} codes 23 properties in every setting; two independent raters agreed on 197/207 codes (kappa 0.92), and an adjudicator settled the rest. Settings are compared only within a phase, so that a difference between training and deployment is never read as a difference between the cultures. In training and in deployment alike, every LLM setting differs from the RL setting on four properties: whether behaviour can be steered through the input, the action set is fixed and known, observations can carry instructions and third parties can author observations. In deployment, every LLM setting also differs from the RL setting on seven more: whether a reward function is defined for the task, reward arrives at every step, the environment computes the reward, observations include the agent's own outputs, the state includes a principal's intent, the environment resets by design and a value estimate selects actions. Whether reward changes the parameters and the parameters change differs between training and deployment in both cultures and not between them. Under process supervision dense reward, Markov prefix, known dynamics and free resets all hold, which is why process supervision is the LLM training setting closest to RL training on those four properties, although its dense reward is a learned process-reward-model score, not an environment signal, and it has no side effects. DeepSeek-R1 reports that it dropped a process reward model after unsuccessful attempts, citing reward hacking, costly step annotation and a more complex pipeline [@deepseekai2025]; @zhang2025 find annotation bias and inflated best-of-N scores in existing process reward models and release an improved one.

0c122c49bdbf6748.paragraph: Two research cultures have grown around the two ends of the table. One begins by positing what is inside the box: an optimiser of a reward R in a decision process the designer wrote down, from which value functions, policy gradients and designed exploration follow [@sutton2018; @schulman2017]. The other treats the inside as unknown: a pretrained model steered by a prompt and a scaffold, judged by what it does on tasks [@yao2023b; @schick2023; @kapoor2024]. @breiman2001 described the same split in statistics. His data-modeling culture begins "Assume that the data are generated by the following model" [@breiman2001]; he put "98% of all statisticians" [@breiman2001] in it; and his objection was that "The conclusions are about the model's mechanism, and not about nature's mechanism." [@breiman2001] His algorithmic culture "considers the inside of the box complex and unknown" [@breiman2001] and validates by predictive accuracy. Table \ref{tab:cultures} sets the four cultures in his lines. We call ours *objective-modeling* and *behavior-modeling*, by their move, not their tribe. The mapping runs the RL-agent culture to Breiman's statistics, not to his machine learning: the move that matters is positing a parametric model of the inside of the box, and an MDP with a reward is such a model. The mapping is of moves, not of people: the same researcher trains a chatbot with PPO in the morning and prompts a tool agent in the afternoon, and the settings table says which culture each act belongs to.

aa7fc5892c52af1f.paragraph: Breiman had a shared scoreboard, test-set accuracy. Agents have task success on benchmarks, and the scoreboard is shared only inside the behavior-modeling culture. Cox's objection transfers directly: "Often the prediction is under quite different conditions from the data" [@breiman2001]. An agent trained in a sandbox with resets and benign tool outputs is deployed without them; the gap between T-AGENT and D-AGENT-X in Table \ref{tab:primitive_cells_deployment} is the gap Cox names. Efron's transfers: "Prediction by itself is only occasionally sufficient." [@breiman2001] A task-success rate says what the agent did on those tasks and nothing about the mechanism, which is what the objective-modeling culture wants to know. Breiman's own Rashomon Effect transfers too: many functions give about the same error rate, so a benchmark score does not identify the agent behind it [@breiman2001; @damour2021]. The analogue we take is Hoadley's. Fair, Isaac ran algorithmic-culture scorecards in production from the 1960s, built from interpretable variables, with constraints on the model's form (monotone scores, shrunken weights) that client demand, law and robustness "led to the concept of score engineering" [@breiman2001]. For agents the constraints sit in the scaffold rather than in the model: the tool set, the permissions and the prompt are what a deployer can write, and the model inside is not read. That placement is our analogy, not Hoadley's. The objective-modeling culture is right that a written constraint is what makes a box usable and wrong about where it must live; the behavior-modeling culture is right that the inside cannot be specified and wrong if it concludes that nothing can be written.

Neither a deployed RL policy nor a deployed LLM uses reward to change its parameters; that difference is between training and deployment, not between the cultures. The reward model, verifier or process reward model is a training artefact: @mclean2026 say of the process reward model that once training is complete it "is no longer used" [@mclean2026], and note that the reward function "is somewhat different from training (updating the policy) to deployment (freezing the policy)" [@mclean2026]. What stands in its place is the instruction in the context, which any later text in the context can revise, and the user's acceptance after the fact.
- **Action and transition.** In T-CHAT and T-RLVR the whole reply is one action and generation leads directly to a terminal state with no subsequent decision: the problem is a contextual bandit [@ahmadian2024; @xiong2024]; the cited work treats RLHF, and we extend the reading to verifier rewards. PPO treats tokens as actions, but the reward is terminal. RLOO and ReMax show that the bandit view suffices and drop the critic [@ahmadian2024; @li2024]; GRPO also drops the critic [@shao2024]. Under process supervision an action is one reasoning step and the transition is deterministic: the agent is the dynamics. In the agent settings an action is a tool call. In agent training the transition is the response of a sandbox the designer builds and resets [@jimenez2024]; in deployment it is what the tool and the world do, which no party fully controls.
- **Observation and state.** In RL the observation is data from a sensor. In the LLM settings the observation is mostly text, and text carries instructions; agents may also receive images and other modalities. In the agent settings tool outputs arrive in the same stream as the user's instructions, and models do not reliably separate the two [@zverev2025; @greshake2023]. The state of a deployed agent includes world state it cannot see and the user's intent; @mclean2026 concede that the agent's inputs "cannot fully capture the true state of the world and the user's intents" [@mclean2026]. In deployment the context window is a bounded, lossy belief.
- **Episode and value.** Resets exist in training. Under process supervision any prefix can be resampled; in agent training the environment resets between tasks. A deployed RL environment may be designed to reset; no LLM deployment setting is. A chatbot's conversation ends, and a tool agent's side effects persist. In deployment neither culture uses a learned value function; in the LLM deployment settings verbal self-checks and retries stand in for it (search-augmented agents score continuations by reverting to earlier states, which a live deployment does not allow), and each probe is a real action with persistent effects.
- **Which settings differ.** Table \ref{tab:gap} codes 23 properties in every setting; two independent raters agreed on 197/207 codes (kappa 0.92), and an adjudicator settled the rest. Settings are compared only within a phase, so that a difference between training and deployment is never read as a difference between the cultures. In training and in deployment alike, every LLM setting differs from the RL setting on four properties: whether behaviour can be steered through the input, the action set is fixed and known, observations can carry instructions and third parties can author observations. In deployment, every LLM setting also differs from the RL setting on seven more: whether a reward function is defined for the task, reward arrives at every step, the environment computes the reward, observations include the agent's own outputs, the state includes a principal's intent, the environment resets by design and a value estimate selects actions. Whether reward changes the parameters and the parameters change differs between training and deployment in both cultures and not between them. Under process supervision dense reward, Markov prefix, known dynamics and free resets all hold, which is why process supervision is the LLM training setting closest to RL training on those four properties, although its dense reward is a learned process-reward-model score, not an environment signal, and it has no side effects. DeepSeek-R1 reports that it dropped a process reward model after unsuccessful attempts, citing reward hacking, costly step annotation and a more complex pipeline [@deepseekai2025]; @zhang2025 find annotation bias and inflated best-of-N scores in existing process reward models and release an improved one.

a1b930207e0380bf.paragraph: Two research cultures have grown around the two ends of the table. One begins by positing what is inside the box: an optimiser of a reward R in a decision process the designer wrote down, from which value functions, policy gradients and designed exploration follow [@sutton2018; @schulman2017]. The other treats the inside as unknown: a pretrained model steered by a prompt and a scaffold, judged by what it does on tasks; it posits a reward only to train the model, and none for the task at deployment [@yao2023b; @schick2023; @kapoor2024]. @breiman2001 described the same split in statistics. His data-modeling culture begins "Assume that the data are generated by the following model" [@breiman2001]; he put "98% of all statisticians" [@breiman2001] in it; and his objection was that "The conclusions are about the model's mechanism, and not about nature's mechanism." [@breiman2001] His algorithmic culture "considers the inside of the box complex and unknown" [@breiman2001] and validates by predictive accuracy. Table \ref{tab:cultures} sets the four cultures in his lines. We call ours *objective-modeling* and *behavior-modeling*, by their move, not their tribe. The mapping runs the RL-agent culture to Breiman's statistics, not to his machine learning: the move that matters is positing a parametric model of the inside of the box, and an MDP with a reward is such a model. The mapping is of moves, not of people: the same researcher trains a chatbot with PPO in the morning and prompts a tool agent in the afternoon, and the settings table says which culture each act belongs to.

8fb90583ef151a0e.paragraph: When an RL researcher and an LLM-agent builder say *agent*, they name different objects, and claims that cross between them arrive with the words but not the objects: a deployed LLM agent is said to hack a reward it does not have. This paper lays the two meanings side by side, one primitive at a time, in training and in deployment, and says where each word keeps its meaning and where it loses it. It describes the gap and proposes no bridge. One culture writes down the decision process and the reward and learns a policy; the other prompts a pretrained model inside a scaffold with tools and judges it by what it does. We take the eight primitives that @sutton2018 define, reward, policy, action, observation, state, transition, episode and value, and read each one in nine settings: an RL agent in training and in deployment, chat training with an outcome reward model, with a verifier and with a process reward model, agent training with trajectory reward, and deployment of a chatbot, of a tool agent with a human between steps and of an autonomous tool agent. The reading is a table of 72 cells, each with its reason and sources. We also code 23 properties in every setting and compare settings only within a phase. In training and in deployment alike, LLM agents differ from RL agents on four properties, among them that an LLM agent's observations can carry instructions and its behaviour can be steered through its input. In deployment the RL agent's task still has a reward function and the LLM's has none. Some differences that look cultural are differences of phase: neither a deployed RL policy nor a deployed LLM uses reward to change its parameters. Chat training with a learned or programmatic outcome reward is a contextual bandit with no subsequent decision and a degenerate value; process supervision has the code of RL training, where both bandit settings do not, on four coded properties, though its per-step reward is a learned score. @breiman2001 described the same split in statistics, between a culture that assumes a stochastic model of the inside of the box and one that treats the inside as unknown and judges by prediction. We set the two cultures of agents in his lines, measure how little the two literatures cite each other, and say which of his discussants' objections transfer: Cox's on prediction under changed conditions, Efron's on prediction being only occasionally sufficient, and Hoadley's on constraints engineered around a model that is not read from the inside.

326eb65036039ca4.paragraph: No prior paper reads the RL primitives setting by setting for LLM systems, or sets the RL-agent culture against the LLM-agent culture. The nearest work comes in four strands. First, the formal reading of RLHF as a bandit: @ahmadian2024 argue that the whole generation should be modelled as a single action and the problem reduces to a bandit; @li2024 drop the value model for the same reason; @xiong2024 formalise RLHF as a KL-regularised contextual bandit; @lambert2025 contrasts the bandit and token-level MDP framings in a textbook. @rafailov2024 show that DPO nonetheless learns an implicit token-level Q-function. Second, the constrained reading of the KL penalty: @moskovitz2024 cast RLHF with several reward models as a constrained MDP with one constraint per reward model, and note that the KL coefficient already acts as a Lagrange multiplier, @gao2023 treat KL as a budget, and @korbak2022 give the competing Bayesian reading. Third, the papers that assert or test the identity between LLM agents and RL agents: @mclean2026 write the agent as a POMDP and offer RL safety tools; our companion paper examines the conditions those tools need [@debunking2026]; @cagatan2026 port the AI safety gridworlds to LLM agents and find specification gaming; @turner2022b argues that a trained policy need not be a reward optimiser. 6f5d1ab66ed11a2d.paragraph:
- **Reward.** In deployment, the RL agent's task still has a reward function, written by its designer, whether or not the frozen policy uses it; the deployed LLM's task has none, and its objective is the instruction in the context. Neither a deployed RL policy nor a deployed LLM uses reward to change its parameters; that difference is between training and deployment, not between the cultures. The reward model, verifier or process reward model is a training artefact: @mclean2026 say of the process reward model that once training is complete it "is no longer used" [@mclean2026], and note that the reward function "is somewhat different from training (updating the policy) to deployment (freezing the policy)" [@mclean2026]. What stands in its place is the instruction in the context, which any later text in the context can revise, and the user's acceptance after the fact.
- **Action and transition.** In T-CHAT and T-RLVR the whole reply is one action and generation leads directly to a terminal state with no subsequent decision: the problem is a contextual bandit [@ahmadian2024; @xiong2024]; the cited work treats RLHF, and we extend the reading to verifier rewards. PPO treats tokens as actions, but the reward is terminal. RLOO and ReMax show that the bandit view suffices and drop the critic [@ahmadian2024; @li2024]; GRPO also drops the critic [@shao2024]. Under process supervision an action is one reasoning step and the transition is deterministic: the agent is the dynamics. In the agent settings an action is a tool call. In agent training the transition is the response of a sandbox the designer builds and resets [@jimenez2024]; in deployment it is what the tool and the world do, which no party fully controls.
- **Observation and state.** In RL the observation is data from a sensor. In the LLM settings the observation is mostly text, and text carries instructions; agents may also receive images and other modalities. In the agent settings tool outputs arrive in the same stream as the user's instructions, and models do not reliably separate the two [@zverev2025; @greshake2023]. The state of a deployed agent includes world state it cannot see and the user's intent; @mclean2026 concede that the agent's inputs "cannot fully capture the true state of the world and the user's intents" [@mclean2026]. In deployment the context window is a bounded, lossy belief.
- **Episode and value.** Resets exist in training. Under process supervision any prefix can be resampled; in agent training the environment resets between tasks. A deployed RL environment may be designed to reset; no LLM deployment setting is. A chatbot's conversation ends, and a tool agent's side effects persist. In deployment neither culture uses a learned value function; in the LLM deployment settings verbal self-checks and retries stand in for it (search-augmented agents score continuations by reverting to earlier states, which a live deployment does not allow), and each probe is a real action with persistent effects.
- **Which settings differ.** Table \ref{tab:gap} codes 23 properties in every setting; two independent raters agreed on 197/207 codes (kappa 0.92), and an adjudicator settled the rest. Settings are compared only within a phase, so that a difference between training and deployment is never read as a difference between the cultures. In training and in deployment alike, every LLM setting differs from the RL setting on four properties: whether behaviour can be steered through the input, the action set is fixed and known, observations can carry instructions and third parties can author observations. In deployment, every LLM setting also differs from the RL setting on seven more: whether a reward function is defined for the task, reward arrives at every step, the environment computes the reward, observations include the agent's own outputs, the state includes a principal's intent, the environment resets by design and a value estimate selects actions. Whether reward changes the parameters and the parameters change differs between training and deployment in both cultures and not between them. Process supervision has the code of RL training, where both bandit settings do not, on four properties: whether reward arrives at every step, an episode has one action, an action is followed by a further decision and a value estimate selects actions; but its per-step reward is a learned process-reward-model score, not an environment signal, and its actions have no side effects. DeepSeek-R1 reports that it dropped a process reward model after unsuccessful attempts, citing reward hacking, costly step annotation and a more complex pipeline [@deepseekai2025]; @zhang2025 find annotation bias and inflated best-of-N scores in existing process reward models and release an improved one.

2911bc9b68916f12.paragraph: Two research cultures have grown around the two ends of the table. One begins by positing what is inside the box: an optimiser of a reward R in a decision process the designer wrote down, from which value functions, policy gradients and designed exploration follow [@sutton2018; @schulman2017]. The other treats the inside as unknown: a pretrained model steered by a prompt and a scaffold, judged by what it does on tasks [@yao2023b; @schick2023; @kapoor2024]; where it posits a reward, it is to train the model, and none is defined for the task at deployment (Table \ref{tab:gap}). @breiman2001 described the same split in statistics. His data-modeling culture begins "Assume that the data are generated by the following model" [@breiman2001]; he put "98% of all statisticians" [@breiman2001] in it; and his objection was that "The conclusions are about the model's mechanism, and not about nature's mechanism." [@breiman2001] His algorithmic culture "considers the inside of the box complex and unknown" [@breiman2001] and validates by predictive accuracy. Table \ref{tab:cultures} sets the four cultures in his lines. We call ours *objective-modeling* and *behavior-modeling*, by their move, not their tribe. The mapping runs the RL-agent culture to Breiman's statistics, not to his machine learning: the move that matters is positing a parametric model of the inside of the box, and an MDP with a reward is such a model. The mapping is of moves, not of people: the same researcher trains a chatbot with PPO in the morning and prompts a tool agent in the afternoon, and the settings table says which culture each act belongs to.

9342b8ebeaf82424.paragraph: Breiman guessed the sizes of his cultures. We measured contact between ours. From OpenAlex [@openalex2026] we built an RL-agent corpus and an LLM-agent corpus for 2012–2026 with general queries (Table \ref{tab:census_general}). Louvain communities on the union graph recover our labels with purity 0.98 on the 1250 works that have at least one citation link (570 isolated works are excluded); the corpora share zero works. dfa1d5662017980a.paragraph: Breiman had a shared scoreboard, test-set accuracy. Agents have task success on benchmarks, and the scoreboard is shared only inside the behavior-modeling culture. Cox's objection transfers directly: "Often the prediction is under quite different conditions from the data" [@breiman2001]. An agent trained in a sandbox with resets and benign tool outputs is deployed without them; the gap between T-AGENT and D-AGENT-X in Table \ref{tab:primitive_cells_deployment} is the gap Cox names. Efron's transfers: "Prediction by itself is only occasionally sufficient." [@breiman2001] A task-success rate says what the agent did on those tasks and nothing about the mechanism, which is what the objective-modeling culture wants to know. Breiman's own Rashomon Effect transfers too: many functions give about the same error rate, so a benchmark score does not identify the agent behind it [@breiman2001; @damour2021]. The analogue we take is Hoadley's. Fair, Isaac ran algorithmic-culture scorecards in production from the 1960s, built from interpretable variables, with constraints on the model's form (monotone scores, shrunken weights) that client demand, law and robustness "led to the concept of score engineering" [@breiman2001]. For agents the constraints sit in the scaffold rather than in the model: the tool set, the permissions and the prompt are what a deployer can write, and the model inside is not read. That placement is our analogy, not Hoadley's. The objective-modeling culture is right that a written constraint is what makes a box usable and wrong about where it must live; the behavior-modeling culture is right that the inside cannot be specified and wrong if it concludes that nothing can be written.

6440e17699bac891.paragraph: When an RL researcher and an LLM-agent builder say *agent*, they name different objects, and claims that cross between them arrive with the words but not the objects: a deployed LLM agent is said to hack a reward it does not have. This paper lays the two meanings side by side, one primitive at a time, in training and in deployment, and says where each word keeps its meaning and where it loses it. It describes the gap and proposes no bridge. One culture writes down the decision process and the reward and learns a policy; the other prompts a pretrained model inside a scaffold with tools and judges it by what it does. We take the eight primitives that @sutton2018 define, reward, policy, action, observation, state, transition, episode and value, and read each one in nine settings: an RL agent in training and in deployment, chat training with an outcome reward model, with a verifier and with a process reward model, agent training with trajectory reward, and deployment of a chatbot, of a tool agent with a human between steps and of an autonomous tool agent. In training and in deployment alike, LLM agents differ from RL agents on four properties, among them that an LLM agent's observations can carry instructions and its behaviour can be steered through its input. In deployment the RL agent's task still has a reward function and the LLM's has none. Some differences that look cultural are differences of phase: neither a deployed RL policy nor a deployed LLM uses reward to change its parameters. Chat training with a learned or programmatic outcome reward is a contextual bandit with no subsequent decision and a degenerate value; process supervision has the code of RL training, where both bandit settings do not, on whether reward arrives at every step, an episode has one action, an action is followed by a further decision and a value estimate selects actions, though its per-step reward is a learned score. @breiman2001 described the same split in statistics, between a culture that assumes a stochastic model of the inside of the box and one that treats the inside as unknown and judges by prediction. a1be22591f0cda8c.paragraph:
- **Reward.** In deployment, the RL agent's task still has a reward function, written by its designer, whether or not the frozen policy uses it; the deployed LLM's task has none, and its objective is the instruction in the context. Neither a deployed RL policy nor a deployed LLM uses reward to change its parameters; that difference is between training and deployment, not between the cultures. The reward model, verifier or process reward model is a training artefact: @mclean2026 say of the process reward model that once training is complete it "is no longer used" [@mclean2026], and note that the reward function "is somewhat different from training (updating the policy) to deployment (freezing the policy)" [@mclean2026]. What stands in its place is the instruction in the context, which any later text in the context can revise, and the user's acceptance after the fact.
- **Action and transition.** In T-CHAT and T-RLVR the whole reply is one action and generation leads directly to a terminal state with no subsequent decision: the problem is a contextual bandit [@ahmadian2024; @xiong2024]; the cited work treats RLHF, and we extend the reading to verifier rewards. PPO treats tokens as actions, but the reward is terminal. RLOO and ReMax show that the bandit view suffices and drop the critic [@ahmadian2024; @li2024]; GRPO also drops the critic [@shao2024]. Under process supervision an action is one reasoning step and the transition is deterministic: the agent is the dynamics. In the agent settings an action is a tool call. In agent training the transition is the response of a sandbox the designer builds and resets [@jimenez2024]; in deployment it is what the tool and the world do, which no party fully controls.
- **Observation and state.** In RL the observation is data from a sensor. In the LLM settings the observation is mostly text, and text carries instructions; agents may also receive images and other modalities. In the agent settings tool outputs arrive in the same stream as the user's instructions, and models do not reliably separate the two [@zverev2025; @greshake2023]. The state of a deployed agent includes world state it cannot see and the user's intent; @mclean2026 concede that the agent's inputs "cannot fully capture the true state of the world and the user's intents" [@mclean2026]. In deployment the context window is a bounded, lossy belief.
- **Episode and value.** Every training setting resets by design. Under process supervision any prefix can be resampled; in agent training the environment resets between tasks. A deployed RL environment may be designed to reset; no LLM deployment setting is. A chatbot's conversation ends, and a tool agent's side effects persist. In deployment neither culture uses a learned value function; in the LLM deployment settings verbal self-checks and retries stand in for it (search-augmented agents score continuations by reverting to earlier states, which a live deployment does not allow), and each probe is a real action with persistent effects.
- **Which settings differ.** Table \ref{tab:gap} codes 23 properties in every setting; two independent raters agreed on 197/207 codes (kappa 0.92), and an adjudicator settled the rest. Settings are compared only within a phase, so that a difference between training and deployment is never read as a difference between the cultures. In training and in deployment alike, every LLM setting differs from the RL setting on four properties: whether behaviour can be steered through the input, the action set is fixed and known, observations can carry instructions and third parties can author observations. In deployment, every LLM setting also differs from the RL setting on seven more: whether a reward function is defined for the task, reward arrives at every step, the environment computes the reward, observations include the agent's own outputs, the state includes a principal's intent, the environment resets by design and a value estimate selects actions. Whether reward changes the parameters and the parameters change differs between training and deployment in both cultures and not between them. Process supervision has the code of RL training, where both bandit settings do not, on four properties: whether reward arrives at every step, an episode has one action, an action is followed by a further decision and a value estimate selects actions; but its per-step reward is a learned process-reward-model score, not an environment signal, and its actions have no side effects. DeepSeek-R1 reports that it dropped a process reward model after unsuccessful attempts, citing reward hacking, costly step annotation and a more complex pipeline [@deepseekai2025]; @zhang2025 find annotation bias and inflated best-of-N scores in existing process reward models and release an improved one.

3b622186e55b7249.paragraph: Two research cultures have grown around the two ends of the table. One begins by positing what is inside the box: an optimiser of a reward R in a decision process the designer wrote down, from which value functions, policy gradients and designed exploration follow [@sutton2018; @schulman2017]. The other treats the inside as unknown: a pretrained model steered by a prompt and a scaffold, judged by what it does on tasks [@yao2023b; @schick2023; @kapoor2024]; where it posits a reward, it is to train the model, and none is defined for the task at deployment (Table \ref{tab:gap}). @breiman2001 described the same split in statistics. His data-modeling culture begins "Assume that the data are generated by the following model" [@breiman2001]; he put "98% of all statisticians" [@breiman2001] in it; and his objection was that "The conclusions are about the model's mechanism, and not about nature's mechanism." [@breiman2001] His algorithmic culture "considers the inside of the box complex and unknown" [@breiman2001] and validates by predictive accuracy. Table \ref{tab:cultures} sets the four cultures in his lines. We call ours *objective-modeling* and *behavior-modeling*, by their move, not their tribe. The mapping runs the RL-agent culture to Breiman's statistics, not to his machine learning: the move that matters is positing a parametric model of the inside of the box, and an MDP with a reward is such a model. The mapping is of moves, not of people: the same researcher trains a chatbot with PPO in the morning and prompts a tool agent in the afternoon, and the settings table says which culture each act belongs to.

9c94990cda01d88b.paragraph: Breiman had a shared scoreboard, test-set accuracy. Agents have task success on benchmarks, and the scoreboard is shared only inside the behavior-modeling culture. Cox's objection transfers directly: "Often the prediction is under quite different conditions from the data" [@breiman2001]. An agent trained in a sandbox that resets, with tool outputs written mostly by its trainer, is deployed without either; the gap between T-AGENT and D-AGENT-X in Table \ref{tab:primitive_cells_deployment} is the gap Cox names. Efron's transfers: "Prediction by itself is only occasionally sufficient." [@breiman2001] A task-success rate says what the agent did on those tasks and nothing about the mechanism, which is what the objective-modeling culture wants to know. Breiman's own Rashomon Effect transfers too: many functions give about the same error rate, so a benchmark score does not identify the agent behind it [@breiman2001; @damour2021]. The analogue we take is Hoadley's. Fair, Isaac ran algorithmic-culture scorecards in production from the 1960s, built from interpretable variables, with constraints on the model's form (monotone scores, shrunken weights) that client demand, law and robustness "led to the concept of score engineering" [@breiman2001]. For agents the constraints sit in the scaffold rather than in the model: the tool set, the permissions and the prompt are what a deployer can write, and the model inside is not read. That placement is our analogy, not Hoadley's. The objective-modeling culture is right that a written constraint is what makes a box usable and wrong about where it must live; the behavior-modeling culture is right that the inside cannot be specified and wrong if it concludes that nothing can be written.

Compared within a phase, LLM agents differ from RL agents in every setting in that their observations can carry instructions and their behaviour can be steered through their input; in deployment their task has no reward function and no designed reset, while a deployed RL agent's task has a reward function and may have a designed reset. Whether reward changes the parameters is a difference of phase, not of culture. Two cultures have grown around the two ends of that table and barely cite each other. Breiman's lesson for them is the one his discussants gave him: prediction under changed conditions is the hard case, a score is only occasionally sufficient, and a box that is not read from the inside is run inside written constraints. e7efae828cb8ec1f.paragraph: When an RL researcher and an LLM-agent builder say *agent*, they name different objects, and claims that cross between them arrive with the words but not the objects: a deployed LLM agent is said to hack a reward it does not have. This paper lays the two meanings side by side, one primitive at a time, in training and in deployment, and says where each word keeps its meaning and where it loses it. It describes the gap and proposes no bridge. One culture writes down the decision process and the reward and learns a policy; the other prompts a pretrained model inside a scaffold with tools and judges it by what it does. We take the eight primitives that @sutton2018 define, reward, policy, action, observation, state, transition, episode and value, and read each one in nine settings: an RL agent in training and in deployment, chat training with an outcome reward model, with a verifier and with a process reward model, agent training with trajectory reward, and deployment of a chatbot, of a tool agent with a human between steps and of an autonomous tool agent. The reading is a table of 72 cells, each with its reason and sources. We also code 23 properties in every setting and compare settings only within a phase. In training and in deployment alike, LLM agents differ from RL agents on four properties, among them that an LLM agent's observations can carry instructions and its behaviour can be steered through its input. In deployment the RL agent's task still has a reward function and the LLM's has none. Some differences that look cultural are differences of phase: neither a deployed RL policy nor a deployed LLM uses reward to change its parameters. Chat training with a learned or programmatic outcome reward is a contextual bandit with no subsequent decision and a degenerate value; process supervision has the code of RL training, where both bandit settings do not, on whether reward arrives at every step, an episode has one action, an action is followed by a further decision and a value estimate selects actions, though its per-step reward is a learned score. @breiman2001 described the same split in statistics, between a culture that assumes a stochastic model of the inside of the box and one that treats the inside as unknown and judges by prediction. We set the two cultures of agents in his lines, measure how little the two literatures cite each other, and say which of his discussants' objections transfer: Cox's on prediction under changed conditions and Efron's on prediction being only occasionally sufficient.

1d9f8282870db132.paragraph: No prior paper reads the RL primitives setting by setting for LLM systems, or sets the RL-agent culture against the LLM-agent culture. The nearest work comes in four strands. First, the formal reading of RLHF as a bandit: @ahmadian2024 argue that the whole generation should be modelled as a single action and the problem reduces to a bandit; @li2024 drop the value model for the same reason; @xiong2024 formalise RLHF as a KL-regularised contextual bandit; @lambert2025 contrasts the bandit and token-level MDP framings in a textbook. @rafailov2024 show that DPO nonetheless learns an implicit token-level Q-function. Second, the constrained reading of the KL penalty: @moskovitz2024 cast RLHF with several reward models as a constrained MDP with one constraint per reward model, and note that the KL coefficient already acts as a Lagrange multiplier, and @korbak2022 give the competing Bayesian reading. Third, the papers that assert or test the identity between LLM agents and RL agents: @mclean2026 write the agent as a POMDP; @turner2022b argues, within RL, that a trained policy need not be a reward optimiser. Fourth, Breiman's frame: @breiman2001, and @damour2021 on the Rashomon set.

a56b7aa86b00afc8.paragraph:
- **Reward.** In deployment, the RL agent's task still has a reward function, written by its designer, whether or not the frozen policy uses it; the deployed LLM's task has none, and its objective is the instruction in the context. Neither a deployed RL policy nor a deployed LLM uses reward to change its parameters; that difference is between training and deployment, not between the cultures. The reward model, verifier or process reward model is a training artefact: @mclean2026 say of the process reward model that once training is complete it "is no longer used" [@mclean2026], and note that the reward function "is somewhat different from training (updating the policy) to deployment (freezing the policy)" [@mclean2026]. What stands in its place is the instruction in the context, which any later text in the context can revise, and the user's acceptance after the fact.
- **Action and transition.** In T-CHAT and T-RLVR the whole reply is one action and generation leads directly to a terminal state with no subsequent decision: the problem is a contextual bandit [@ahmadian2024; @xiong2024]; the cited work treats RLHF, and we extend the reading to verifier rewards. PPO treats tokens as actions, but the reward is terminal. RLOO and ReMax show that the bandit view suffices and drop the critic [@ahmadian2024; @li2024]; GRPO also drops the critic [@shao2024]. Under process supervision an action is one reasoning step and the transition is deterministic: the agent is the dynamics. In the agent settings an action is a tool call. In agent training the transition is the response of a sandbox the designer builds and resets [@jimenez2024]; in deployment it is what the tool and the world do, which no party fully controls.
- **Observation and state.** In RL the observation is data from a sensor. In the LLM settings the observation is mostly text, and text carries instructions; agents may also receive images and other modalities. In the agent settings tool outputs arrive in the same stream as the user's instructions, and models do not reliably separate the two [@zverev2025; @greshake2023]. The state of a deployed agent includes world state it cannot see and the user's intent; @mclean2026 concede that the agent's inputs "cannot fully capture the true state of the world and the user's intents" [@mclean2026]. In deployment the context window is a bounded, lossy belief.
- **Episode and value.** Every training setting resets by design. Under process supervision any prefix can be resampled; in agent training the environment resets between tasks. A deployed RL environment may be designed to reset; no LLM deployment setting is. A chatbot's conversation ends, and a tool agent's side effects persist. In deployment neither culture uses a learned value function; in the LLM deployment settings verbal self-checks and retries stand in for it (search-augmented agents score continuations by reverting to earlier states, which a live deployment does not allow), and each probe is a real action with persistent effects.
- **Which settings differ.** Table \ref{tab:gap} codes 23 properties in every setting; two independent raters agreed on 197/207 codes (kappa 0.92), and an adjudicator settled the rest. Settings are compared only within a phase, so that a difference between training and deployment is never read as a difference between the cultures. In training and in deployment alike, every LLM setting differs from the RL setting on four properties: whether behaviour can be steered through the input, the action set is fixed and known, observations can carry instructions and third parties can author observations. In deployment, every LLM setting also differs from the RL setting on seven more: whether a reward function is defined for the task, reward arrives at every step, the environment computes the reward, observations include the agent's own outputs, the state includes a principal's intent, the environment resets by design and a value estimate selects actions. Whether reward changes the parameters and the parameters change differs between training and deployment in both cultures and not between them. Process supervision has the code of RL training, where both bandit settings do not, on four properties: whether reward arrives at every step, an episode has one action, an action is followed by a further decision and a value estimate selects actions; but its per-step reward is a learned process-reward-model score, not an environment signal, and its actions have no side effects.

ca2c06a17bfba85b.paragraph: When an RL researcher and an LLM-agent builder say *agent*, they name different objects, and claims that cross between them arrive with the words but not the objects: a deployed LLM agent is said to hack a reward it does not have. This paper lays the two meanings side by side, one primitive at a time, in training and in deployment, and says where each word keeps its meaning and where it loses it. It describes the gap and proposes no bridge. One culture writes down the decision process and the reward and learns a policy; the other prompts a pretrained model inside a scaffold with tools and judges it by what it does. We take the eight primitives that @sutton2018 define, reward, policy, action, observation, state, transition, episode and value, and read each one in nine settings: an RL agent in training and in deployment, chat training with an outcome reward model, with a verifier and with a process reward model, agent training with trajectory reward, and deployment of a chatbot, of a tool agent with a human between steps and of an autonomous tool agent. The reading is a table of 72 cells, each with its reason, and sources where the reason rests on one. We also code 23 properties in every setting and compare settings only within a phase. In training and in deployment alike, LLM agents differ from RL agents on five properties, among them that an LLM agent's observations can carry instructions and its behaviour can be steered by instructions in its input. In deployment the RL agent's task still has a reward function and the LLM's has none. Some differences that look cultural are differences of phase: neither a deployed RL policy nor a deployed LLM uses reward to change its parameters. Chat training with a learned or programmatic outcome reward is a contextual bandit with no subsequent decision and a degenerate value, for which the critic is often dropped; process supervision has the code of RL training, where both bandit settings do not, on whether reward arrives at every step, an episode has one action, an action is followed by a further decision and a value estimate selects actions, though its per-step reward is a learned score. @breiman2001 described the same split in statistics, between a culture that assumes a stochastic model of the inside of the box and one that treats the inside as unknown and judges by prediction. We set the two cultures of agents in his lines, measure how little the two literatures cite each other, and say which of his discussants' objections transfer: Cox's on prediction under changed conditions and Efron's on prediction being only occasionally sufficient.

4addc52a41dfead2.paragraph: No prior paper reads the RL primitives setting by setting for LLM systems, or sets the RL-agent culture against the LLM-agent culture. The nearest work comes in four strands. First, the formal reading of RLHF as a bandit: @ahmadian2024 argue that the whole generation should be modelled as a single action and the problem reduces to a bandit; @li2024 drop the value model for the same reason; @xiong2024 formalise RLHF as a KL-regularised contextual bandit; @lambert2025 contrasts the bandit and token-level MDP framings in a textbook. @rafailov2024 show that DPO nonetheless learns an implicit token-level Q-function. Second, the constrained reading of the KL penalty: @moskovitz2024 cast RLHF with several reward models as a constrained MDP with one constraint per reward model, and note that the KL coefficient already acts as a Lagrange multiplier, and @korbak2022 give the competing Bayesian reading. Third, the paper that asserts the identity between LLM agents and RL agents: @mclean2026 write the agent as a POMDP. On the reward primitive, @turner2022b argues, within RL, that a trained policy need not be a reward optimiser. Fourth, Breiman's frame: @breiman2001, and @damour2021 on the Rashomon set.

35a9720f1be90414.paragraph:
- **Reward.** In deployment, the RL agent's task still has a reward function, written by its designer, whether or not the frozen policy uses it; the deployed LLM's task has none, and its objective is the instruction in the context. Neither a deployed RL policy nor a deployed LLM uses reward to change its parameters; that difference is between training and deployment, not between the cultures. The reward model, verifier or process reward model is a training artefact: @mclean2026 say of the process reward model that once training is complete it "is no longer used" [@mclean2026], and note that the reward function "is somewhat different from training (updating the policy) to deployment (freezing the policy)" [@mclean2026]. What stands in its place is the instruction in the context, which any later text in the context can revise, and the user's acceptance after the fact.
- **Action and transition.** In T-CHAT and T-RLVR the whole reply is one action and generation leads directly to a terminal state with no subsequent decision: the problem is a contextual bandit [@ahmadian2024; @xiong2024]; the cited work treats RLHF, and we extend the reading to verifier rewards. PPO treats tokens as actions, but the reward is terminal. RLOO and ReMax show that the bandit view suffices and drop the critic [@ahmadian2024; @li2024]; GRPO also drops the critic [@shao2024]. Under process supervision an action is one reasoning step and the transition is deterministic: the agent is the dynamics. In the agent settings an action is a tool call. In agent training the transition is the response of an environment the designer builds and restarts for each episode [@zhou2024b]; in deployment it is what the tool and the world do, which no party fully controls.
- **Observation and state.** In RL the observation is data from a sensor. In the LLM settings the observation is mostly text, and text carries instructions; agents may also receive images and other modalities. In the agent settings tool outputs arrive in the same stream as the user's instructions, and models do not reliably separate the two [@zverev2025; @greshake2023]. The state of a deployed agent includes world state it cannot see and the user's intent; @mclean2026 concede that the agent's inputs "cannot fully capture the true state of the world and the user's intents" [@mclean2026]. In deployment the context window is a bounded, lossy belief.
- **Episode and value.** Every training setting resets by design. Under process supervision any prefix can be resampled; in agent training the environment resets between tasks. A deployed RL environment may be designed to reset; no LLM deployment setting is. A chatbot's conversation ends, and a tool agent's side effects persist. In deployment no LLM setting uses a learned value function, and a deployed RL policy uses one only when it is value-based (a fixed Q-network, or search with a learned value); in the LLM deployment settings verbal self-checks and retries stand in for it (search-augmented agents score continuations by reverting to earlier states, which a live deployment does not allow), and each probe is a real action with persistent effects.
- **Which settings differ.** Table \ref{tab:gap} codes 23 properties in every setting; two independent LLM raters (instances of Claude Sonnet) agreed on 197/207 codes (kappa 0.92), and a further instance, as adjudicator, settled the rest. Settings are compared only within a phase, so that a difference between training and deployment is never read as a difference between the cultures. In training and in deployment alike, every LLM setting differs from the RL setting on five properties: whether behaviour can be steered by instructions in the input, the action set is fixed and known, observations can carry instructions, third parties can author observations and a learned value function is used. In deployment, every LLM setting also differs from the RL setting on seven more: whether a reward function is defined for the task, reward arrives at every step, the environment computes the reward, observations include the agent's own outputs, the state includes a principal's intent, the environment resets by design and a value estimate selects actions. Whether reward changes the parameters and the parameters change differs between training and deployment in both cultures and not between them. Process supervision has the code of RL training, where both bandit settings do not, on four properties: whether reward arrives at every step, an episode has one action, an action is followed by a further decision and a value estimate selects actions; but its per-step reward is a learned process-reward-model score, not an environment signal, and its actions have no side effects.

51ec45acc6300829.paragraph: Two research cultures have grown around the two ends of the table. One begins by positing what is inside the box: an optimiser of a reward R in a decision process the designer wrote down, from which value functions, policy gradients and designed exploration follow [@sutton2018; @schulman2017]. The other treats the inside as unknown: a pretrained model steered by a prompt and a scaffold, judged by what it does on tasks [@yao2023b; @kapoor2024]; where it posits a reward, it is to train the model, and none is defined for the task at deployment (Table \ref{tab:gap}). @breiman2001 described the same split in statistics. His data-modeling culture begins "Assume that the data are generated by the following model" [@breiman2001]; he put "98% of all statisticians" [@breiman2001] in it; and his objection was that "The conclusions are about the model's mechanism, and not about nature's mechanism." [@breiman2001] His algorithmic culture "considers the inside of the box complex and unknown" [@breiman2001] and validates by predictive accuracy. Table \ref{tab:cultures} sets the four cultures in his lines. We call ours *objective-modeling* and *behavior-modeling*, by their move, not their tribe. The mapping runs the RL-agent culture to Breiman's statistics, not to his machine learning: the move that matters is positing a parametric model of the inside of the box, and an MDP with a reward is such a model. The mapping is of moves, not of people: the same researcher trains a chatbot with PPO in the morning and prompts a tool agent in the afternoon, and the settings table says which culture each act belongs to.

In the behavior-modeling culture, task-success rates on benchmarks are a principal way to judge agents. Cox's objection transfers directly: "Often the prediction is under quite different conditions from the data" [@breiman2001]. Efron's transfers: "Prediction by itself is only occasionally sufficient." [@breiman2001] A task-success rate says what the agent did on those tasks and nothing about the mechanism, which is what the objective-modeling culture wants to know. Breiman's own Rashomon Effect transfers too: many functions give about the same error rate, so a benchmark score does not identify the agent behind it [@breiman2001; @damour2021].

537264f47ef11e53.paragraph: When an RL researcher and an LLM-agent builder say *agent*, they name different objects, and claims that cross between them arrive with the words but not the objects: a deployed LLM agent is said to hack a reward it does not have. This paper lays the two meanings side by side, one primitive at a time, in training and in deployment, and says where each word keeps its meaning and where it loses it. It describes the gap and proposes no bridge. One culture writes down the decision process and the reward and learns a policy; the other prompts a pretrained model inside a scaffold with tools and judges it by what it does. We take the eight primitives that @sutton2018 define, reward, policy, action, observation, state, transition, episode and value, and read each one in nine settings: an RL agent in training and in deployment, chat training with an outcome reward model, with a verifier and with a process reward model, agent training with trajectory reward, and deployment of a chatbot, of a tool agent with a human between steps and of an autonomous tool agent. The reading is a table of 72 cells, each with its reason, and sources where the reason rests on one. We also code 23 properties in every setting and compare settings only within a phase. In training and in deployment alike, LLM agents differ from RL agents on six properties, among them that an LLM agent's observations can carry instructions and its behaviour can be steered by instructions in its input. In deployment the RL agent's task still has a reward function and the LLM's has none. Some differences that look cultural are differences of phase: neither a deployed RL policy nor a deployed LLM uses reward to change its parameters. Chat training with a learned or programmatic outcome reward is a contextual bandit with no subsequent decision and a degenerate value, for which the critic is often dropped; process supervision has the code of RL training, where both bandit settings do not, on whether reward arrives at every step, an episode has one action and an action is followed by a further decision, though its per-step reward is a learned score. @breiman2001 described the same split in statistics, between a culture that assumes a stochastic model of the inside of the box and one that treats the inside as unknown and judges by prediction. We set the two cultures of agents in his lines, measure how little the two literatures cite each other, and say which of his discussants' objections transfer: Cox's on prediction under changed conditions and Efron's on prediction being only occasionally sufficient.

624d62de75c8810c.paragraph: No prior paper reads the RL primitives setting by setting for LLM systems, or sets the RL-agent culture against the LLM-agent culture. The nearest work comes in four strands. First, the formal reading of RLHF as a bandit: @ahmadian2024 argue that the whole generation should be modelled as a single action and the problem reduces to a bandit; @li2024 drop the value model for the same reason; @xiong2024 formalise RLHF as a KL-regularised contextual bandit; @lambert2025 contrasts the bandit and token-level MDP framings in a textbook. @rafailov2024 show that DPO nonetheless learns an implicit token-level Q-function. Second, the constrained reading of the KL penalty: @moskovitz2024 cast RLHF with several reward models as a constrained MDP with one constraint per reward model, and note that the KL coefficient already acts as a Lagrange multiplier, and @korbak2022 give the competing Bayesian reading. Third, the paper that states the equivalence: @mclean2026 "formalize the problem equivalence" [@mclean2026] between AI agents and RL agents and write the agent as a POMDP. On the reward primitive, @turner2022b argues, within RL, that a trained policy need not be a reward optimiser. Fourth, Breiman's frame: @breiman2001, and @damour2021 on the Rashomon set.

7aa2fecfb8ecbe7b.paragraph: Two research cultures have grown around the two ends of the table. One begins by positing what is inside the box: an optimiser of a reward R in a decision process the designer wrote down, from which value functions, policy gradients and designed exploration follow [@sutton2018; @schulman2017]. The other treats the inside as unknown: a pretrained model steered by a prompt and a scaffold, judged by what it does on tasks [@yao2023b; @kapoor2024]; where it posits a reward, it is to train the model, and none is defined for the task at deployment (Table \ref{tab:gap}). @breiman2001 described the same split in statistics. His data-modeling culture begins "Assume that the data are generated by the following model" [@breiman2001]; he put "98% of all statisticians" [@breiman2001] in it; and his objection was that "The conclusions are about the model's mechanism, and not about nature's mechanism." [@breiman2001] His algorithmic culture "considers the inside of the box complex and unknown" [@breiman2001] and validates by predictive accuracy. Table \ref{tab:cultures} sets the four cultures in his lines. We call ours *objective-modeling* and *behavior-modeling*, by their move, not their tribe. The mapping runs the RL-agent culture to Breiman's statistics, not to his machine learning: in our reading, the move that matters is writing down a model before looking at behaviour: the RL-agent culture writes down a decision process and a reward, as Breiman's data-modeling culture writes down a stochastic data model. The mapping is of moves, not of people: the same researcher may write down a decision process and a reward in the morning and prompt a tool agent in the afternoon. Our comparisons are between settings: T-RL and D-RL stand for the RL-agent culture, and every chat and agent setting, training included, stands for the LLM-agent culture, although chat and agent training use RL algorithms.

537b8a88abbe5b9c.paragraph: In Breiman's account the algorithmic culture validates a model by predictive accuracy, and the data-modeling culture by goodness-of-fit tests and residual examination [@breiman2001]. In the behavior-modeling culture, task-success rates on benchmarks are a principal way to judge agents. Cox's objection transfers directly: "Often the prediction is under quite different conditions from the data" [@breiman2001]. An agent trained in a sandbox that resets, where third parties author tool outputs at most in part, is deployed where nothing resets and third parties can author them; the gap between T-AGENT (Table \ref{tab:primitive_cells_training}) and D-AGENT-X (Table \ref{tab:primitive_cells_deployment}) is the gap Cox names. Efron's transfers: "Prediction by itself is only occasionally sufficient." [@breiman2001] A task-success rate says what the agent did on those tasks and nothing about the mechanism, which is what the objective-modeling culture wants to know. Breiman's own Rashomon Effect transfers too: many functions give about the same error rate, so a benchmark score does not identify the agent behind it [@breiman2001; @damour2021].

Whether reward changes the parameters is a difference of phase, not of culture. Two cultures have grown around the two ends of that table and barely cite each other. Two of Breiman's discussants' objections transfer to them: prediction under changed conditions is the hard case, and a score is only occasionally sufficient.
